  - demand for on-the-fly LLM services -> address these issues
  - optimize LLMs for constrained devices + innovate on wireless side
  - collaborative approach: local computation on mobile devices + offload intensive tasks to servers

  - servers allocate wireless + computational resources: bandwidth, user/server transmit power, GPU computing resources -> parameters sent back to users

  - simulations show DASHF effective

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are spreading quickly, and they are a monumental leap for artificial intelligence and natural language processing. These models have deep structures and vast parameter sizes, and they offer capabilities that redefine the benchmarks of machine-human interactions for 6G. But because they are so big and intricate, they cannot be deployed effortlessly, especially in constrained environments like mobile devices.

Mobile edge computing (MEC) environments are designed to bring computation closer to the data source, so they seem like a perfect fit for deploying LLMs. Still, MEC has its own set of challenges. Mobile devices are constrained by computational resources and battery life, and this makes it strenuous to run these heavyweight LLMs efficiently. Also, wireless communication is unpredictable, with fluctuating data rates and potential for high latency, and this complicates the integration of LLMs.

## I-A Related Work

In this section, we briefly introduce some recent research on combining LLM and MEC.

Recent advancements in LLMs and foundation models have pushed natural language processing and artificial intelligence (AI) tasks forward a lot, and MEC plays a crucial role in reducing latency and boosting efficiency. One example is the computing and network convergence (CNC) brain, which uses AI to match resources in computing and network convergence environments. It shows a trend towards more autonomous, self-optimizing networks that are suitable for Internet of things (IoT) and advanced smart applications.

At the same time, in federated learning, PromptFL was introduced and it is a significant leap. This method changes federated learning by using prompt training in environments with limited resources, which improves processing efficiency and gives better resource distribution in distributed computing setups. PromptFL shows that there is a critical need for AI systems that are adaptable and scalable, especially in dynamic network environments.

Also, Generative AI is being combined with mobile edge networks in 6G communications, as discussed in, and this opens new avenues for enhancing network intelligence and efficiency, especially when resources are limited. This integration hints at future generative mobile edge networks, which could lead to more robust, intelligent, and self-learning network systems, and could boost user experiences and operational efficiency in a variety of sectors.

## I-B Challenges and motivations

There is a growing demand for on-the-fly LLM services, and to meet it we need to address these issues. This means optimizing the LLMs for constrained devices and also innovating on the wireless communication side. A potential solution is a collaborative approach, where local computations on mobile devices are complemented by offloading specific, intensive tasks to servers that are more capable. This kind of paradigm can make LLMs in MEC environments a tangible reality.

At present there are few or no papers on user connection and communication computing resource allocation using MEC for assisting network training in LLM scenarios.

## I-C Studied problem
  - LLM-driven MEC system; user service-cost ratio (SCR) = \frac{\text{service score}}{\text{cost}}
  - balance of service score vs delay and energy consumption
  - service score: user's wireless + computational resources as perceived by server
  - cost: cumulative delay + energy of users and servers
  - users train initial adapter layers on local data -> send parameters to servers -> servers train subsequent layers
  - servers allocate wireless + computational resources: bandwidth, user/server transmit power, GPU computing resources -> parameters sent back to users
## I-D Main contributions
  - first to study user association + resource allocation in LLM wireless communication scenario
  - joint optimization of user-server adapter parameter training ratio and user association
  - SCR: service scores vs delay/energy in uplink + downlink; trade-off metric
  - DASHF: Dinkelbach, alternating optimization, SDR, Hungarian, novel FP technique (cite, IEEE JSAC); rewrite as QCQP; first user connections + training ratios as one QCQP, then communication-computation resource allocation (bandwidth, transmit power, computing frequency) for non-convex FP problem
  - simulations show DASHF effective
- Organization: Sec. II system model + problem; III DASHF; IV complexity; V numerical results; VI conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are spreading quickly, and they are a monumental leap for artificial intelligence and natural language processing. These models have deep structures and vast parameter sizes, and they offer capabilities that redefine the benchmarks of machine-human interactions for 6G. But because they are so big and intricate, they cannot be deployed effortlessly, especially in constrained environments like mobile devices.

Mobile edge computing (MEC) environments are designed to bring computation closer to the data source, so they seem like a perfect fit for deploying LLMs. Still, MEC has its own set of challenges. Mobile devices are constrained by computational resources and battery life, and this makes it strenuous to run these heavyweight LLMs efficiently. Also, wireless communication is unpredictable, with fluctuating data rates and potential for high latency, and this complicates the integration of LLMs.

## I-A Related Work

In this section, we briefly introduce some recent research on combining LLM and MEC.

Recent advancements in LLMs and foundation models have pushed natural language processing and artificial intelligence (AI) tasks forward a lot, and MEC plays a crucial role in reducing latency and boosting efficiency. One example is the computing and network convergence (CNC) brain, which uses AI to match resources in computing and network convergence environments. It shows a trend towards more autonomous, self-optimizing networks that are suitable for Internet of things (IoT) and advanced smart applications.

At the same time, in federated learning, PromptFL was introduced and it is a significant leap. This method changes federated learning by using prompt training in environments with limited resources, which improves processing efficiency and gives better resource distribution in distributed computing setups. PromptFL shows that there is a critical need for AI systems that are adaptable and scalable, especially in dynamic network environments.

Also, Generative AI is being combined with mobile edge networks in 6G communications, as discussed in, and this opens new avenues for enhancing network intelligence and efficiency, especially when resources are limited. This integration hints at future generative mobile edge networks, which could lead to more robust, intelligent, and self-learning network systems, and could boost user experiences and operational efficiency in a variety of sectors.

## I-B Challenges and motivations

There is a growing demand for on-the-fly LLM services, and to meet it we need to address these issues. This means optimizing the LLMs for constrained devices and also innovating on the wireless communication side. A potential solution is a collaborative approach, where local computations on mobile devices are complemented by offloading specific, intensive tasks to servers that are more capable. This kind of paradigm can make LLMs in MEC environments a tangible reality.

At present there are few or no papers on user connection and communication computing resource allocation using MEC for assisting network training in LLM scenarios.

## I-C Studied problem

In this paper, we study the LLM-driven MEC system and we introduce a new concept called the user service-cost ratio (SCR), represented as \frac{\text{service score}}{\text{cost}}. This metric captures the balance between user service scores and the factors of delay and energy consumption in mobile computing environments. The user service score combines a user's wireless and computational resources as perceived by the server. Cost consumption is the cumulative delay and energy expenditure of both users and servers. Because LLMs are computationally challenging, we assume that users first train the initial layers of the adapters with their local data. After this preliminary training is done, users send these trained parameters to the servers. Servers have more computational resources, so they take over from here and train the subsequent layers of the adapters. Specifically, servers then assign wireless and computational resources to each user. This includes bandwidth, user and server transmission power, and the GPU computing resources of users and servers. When this is complete, the servers send the refined parameters back to the users.

## I-D Main contributions

As far as we know, our paper is the first to explore user association and resource allocation in the LLM wireless communication scenario. Our contributions include a new joint optimization problem, the concept of SCR, and a new alternating optimization algorithm, as follows:

\bullet Joint Optimization of User-Sercer Adapter Parameter Training Ratio and User Association: We propose a joint optimization problem that optimizes user adapter training offloading and user association for tailored LLM service to users.

\bullet Introduction of the User Service-Cost Ratio: We introduce the concept of the user service-cost ratio (SCR). SCR quantifies the balance between user service scores and the overall delay and energy consumption in the whole uplink and downlink communication. It is a useful metric for assessing the trade-off between the service resources a user obtains and resource efficiency.

\bullet Innovative Alternating Optimization Approach: We propose an Alternating Optimization (AO) approach called DASHF, which is the combination of the D inkelbach algorithm, a lternating optimization, s emidefinite relaxation (SDR), the H ungarian algorithm, and a new f ractional programming (FP) technique by published in IEEE JSAC recently. The hardest part of DASHF is rewriting an optimization problem as Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Programming (QCQP) through carefully constructed transformations, so that SDR and the Hungarian algorithm can be used to get a solution. First, it handles the optimization of user connections and adapter parameter training ratios as a single QCQP problem. Then it handles the optimization of communication-computation resource allocation (for bandwidth, transmit power of users and servers, and computing frequency of users and servers), and gives an effective solution for the non-convex FP problem.

\bullet The simulation results show that the proposed DASHF algorithm is effective in achieving the joint optimization of user adapter parameter offloading, resource allocation, service-cost ratio, and resource allocation, which shows its practical applicability and benefits.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system model and optimization problem formulation. Section III proposes the DASHF algorithm to solve the optimization problem. Section IV analyzes the complexity of DASHF. Section V gives the numerical results. Section VI concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) marks a monumental leap in artificial intelligence and natural language processing. These models, with their deep structures and vast parameter sizes, offer capabilities that redefine the benchmarks of machine-human interactions for 6G [1]. However, their size and intricacy mean they cannot be effortlessly deployed, especially in constrained environments like mobile devices [2].

Mobile edge computing (MEC) environments, designed to bring computation closer to the data source, seem like a perfect fit for deploying LLMs. Still, they present their own set of challenges. Mobile devices are constrained by computational resources and battery life, making it strenuous to run these heavyweight LLMs efficiently [3]. Additionally, the unpredictability of wireless communication, with its fluctuating data rates and potential for high latency, complicates the seamless integration of LLMs [4].

## I-A Related Work

In this section, we briefly introduce some recent research on the combination of LLM and MEC.

Recent advancements in LLMs and foundation models have markedly propelled natural language processing and artificial intelligence (AI) tasks, with MEC playing a crucial role in reducing latency and boosting efficiency. Among these, the computing and network convergence (CNC) brain [5] stands out, using AI to effectively match resources in computing and network convergence environments and showing a trend towards more autonomous, self-optimizing networks suitable for Internet of things (IoT) and advanced smart applications.

Simultaneously, in federated learning, the introduction of PromptFL [6] represents a significant leap. This method changes federated learning by adopting prompt training in environments with limited resources, improving processing efficiency and ensuring better resource distribution in distributed computing setups. PromptFL's emergence underlines the critical need for AI systems that are both adaptable and scalable, especially in dynamic network environments.

Additionally, the fusion of Generative AI with mobile edge networks in 6G communications, as discussed in [7], opens new avenues for enhancing network intelligence and efficiency, especially in scenarios with limited resources. This integration hints at future developments in generative mobile edge networks, which could lead to more robust, intelligent, and self-learning network systems, boosting user experiences and operational efficiency in a variety of sectors.

## I-B Challenges and motivations

To meet the growing demand for on-the-fly LLM services, there is a pressing need to address these issues. This involves optimizing the LLMs for constrained devices and innovating on the wireless communication front. A potential solution lies in a collaborative approach, where local computations on mobile devices are complemented by offloading specific, intensive tasks to more capable servers. Such a paradigm can make the promise of LLMs in MEC environments a tangible reality.

At present, there are few or no papers on user connection and communication computing resource allocation using MEC for assisting network training in LLM scenarios.

## I-C Studied problem

In this paper, we explore the LLM-driven MEC system and introduce the novel concept of the user service-cost ratio (SCR), represented as \frac{\text{service score}}{\text{cost}}. This metric captures the balance between user service scores and the crucial factors of delay and energy consumption within mobile computing environments. The user service score combines a user's wireless and computational resources as perceived by the server. Cost consumption embodies the cumulative delay and energy expenditure of both users and servers. Given the computational challenges posed by LLMs, we hypothesize that users begin by training the initial layers of the adapters with their local data. Once this preliminary training is completed, users send the trained parameters to the servers. Servers, equipped with more computational resources, take over from this point and train the subsequent layers of the adapters. Specifically, servers assign both wireless and computational resources to each user, including bandwidth, user and server transmission power, and the GPU computing resources of users and servers. Upon completion, the refined parameters are relayed back to the users by the servers.

## I-D Main contributions

To the best of our knowledge, our paper is the first to explore user association and resource allocation in the LLM wireless communication scenario. Our contributions include a novel joint optimization problem, the concept of SCR, and a novel alternating optimization algorithm as follows:

\bullet Joint Optimization of User-Sercer Adapter Parameter Training Ratio and User Association: We propose a joint optimization problem that optimizes user adapter training offloading and user association for tailored LLM service to users.

\bullet Introduction of the User Service-Cost Ratio: The concept of the user service-cost ratio (SCR) is introduced. SCR quantifies the balance between user service scores and the overall delay and energy consumption in the entire uplink and downlink communication. It provides a valuable metric for assessing the trade-off between the user's obtained service resources and resource efficiency.

\bullet Innovative Alternating Optimization Approach: We propose an innovative Alternating Optimization (AO) approach called DASHF, which combines the D inkelbach algorithm, a lternating optimization, s emidefinite relaxation (SDR), the H ungarian algorithm, and a novel f ractional programming (FP) technique by [8] recently published in IEEE JSAC. The most challenging part of DASHF is rewriting an optimization problem as Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Programming (QCQP) via carefully constructed transformations, in order to leverage SDR and the Hungarian algorithm to obtain a solution. It first addresses the optimization of user connections and adapter parameter training ratios as a single QCQP problem. It then turns to the optimization of communication-computation resource allocation (for bandwidth, transmit power of users and servers, and computing frequency of users and servers), providing an effective solution for the non-convex FP problem.

\bullet The simulation results substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed DASHF algorithm in achieving the joint optimization of user adapter parameter offloading, resource allocation, service-cost ratio, and resource allocation, demonstrating its practical applicability and benefits.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The system model and optimization problem formulation are presented in Section II. We propose the DASHF algorithm to solve the optimization problem in Section III. The complexity of DASHF is analyzed in Section IV. The numerical results are provided in Section V, and we conclude the paper in Section VI.

References:
